'''''Acacia salicina''''' is a thornless species of ''[[Acacia]]'' native to [[Australia]]. It is a large [[shrub]] or small evergreen<ref name="edu">[http://e-commerce.pvc.maricopa.edu/cis234/jsummers/Final/PlantList.xml Gardens At Carefree Town Center - Plant Identification List] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080408234903/http://e-commerce.pvc.maricopa.edu/cis234/jsummers/Final/PlantList.xml |date=April 8, 2008 }}</ref> [[tree]] growing up to 13.7 m (45 ft) tall. It is a fast grower, dropping lots of [[leaf litter]], with a life span of about 10–50 years. In its native range, ''A. salicina'' flowers from February to June.<ref name=plantnet>{{Cite web |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Acacia~salicina |title=NSW Flora Online: ''Acacia salicina'' |access-date=2024-06-06}}</ref> In the [[Northern Hemisphere]], ''A. salicina'' flowers primarily from October to January and the seed pods are often visible from April to July.<ref>[http://cals.arizona.edu/pubs/crops/az1359/az13592b.pdf PDF] Ursula K. Schuch and Margaret Norem, Growth of Legume Tree Species
Growing in the Southwestern United States, University of Arizona.</ref> The tree's seeds are shiny, black and have a crimson appendage-like [[aril]].<ref name="species">{{Cite web|url=http://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/species-bank/sbank-treatment2.pl?id=2006|title=Species Bank Treatment for Acacia Salicina|website=Environment.gov.au|access-date=15 March 2022}}</ref>
''A. salicina'' is "closely related" to ''[[Acacia ligulata]]''<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/texhtml.cgi?form=speciesfacts&keyname=Acacia+ligulata |title=Fact Sheet for Acacia ligulata |access-date=2007-06-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070829011447/http://flora.sa.gov.au/cgi-bin/texhtml.cgi?form=speciesfacts&keyname=Acacia+ligulata |archive-date=2007-08-29 |url-status=dead }}</ref> and ''[[Acacia bivenosa]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.worldwidewattle.com/speciesgallery/ligulata.php|title=Acacia ligulata - WATTLE|website=Worldwidewattle.com|access-date=15 March 2022}}</ref>

==Naming==
The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''salicina'' refers to its pendulous, willow-like (genus ''Salix'') habit. 
Common names include '''cooba''', '''native willow''', '''willow wattle''', '''Broughton willow''', '''sally wattle''', '''black sallee''' and '''black wattle'''. The [[Wiradjuri]] people of [[New South Wales]] use the name ''Guba''.<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Williams |editor1-first=Alice |editor2-last=Sides |editor2-first=Tim |date=2008 |title=Wiradjuri Plant Use in the Murrumbidgee Catchment |publisher=Murrumbidgee Catchment Management Authority |page=10 |isbn=978-0-7347-5856-9}}</ref> The 1889 book, ''The Useful Native Plants of Australia'', records that common names included native willow and Broughton willow near the Broughton River in South Australia. It also records it was called ''Cooba'' or ''Kooba'' by [[Indigenous Australians|Indigenous people]] in Western New South Wales and ''Motherumba'' by those on the Castlereagh River, New South Wales.<ref name="J. H. Maiden 1889"/>

==Description==
''Acacia salicina'' is an erect or spreading shrub or tree 3–10 metres high, sometimes to 20 m, which often suckers freely. The bark is finely fissured and brownish. The branchlets are pendent, angled or flattened towards the apices, and [[Glabrousness| glabrous]].<ref name=plantnet/> 
The [[phyllode]]s are pendent, narrowly elliptic to narrowly [[Glossary of leaf morphology#oblanceolate|oblanceolate]], straight or slightly curved, usually 5–16.5 cm long and 5–12 mm wide and glabrous. The phyllodes have a prominent midvein and are penniveined with a [[wikt:mucro|mucro]] at the apex. They have 2–5 small glands along the margin and the [[pulvinus]] is 1–3 mm long.<ref name=plantnet/>
There are usually 1-8 [[inflorescence]]s in an axillary raceme with axis 0.5–6 cm long. The [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncles]] are 4–15 mm long and glabrous. The flower heads are globose, 15–30-flowered, 7–10 mm in diameter, and pale yellow to white.<ref name=plantnet/>
The seed pods are straight or slightly curved, roughly flat, straight-sided to irregularly constricted between the seeds, 3–12 cm long and 7–13 mm wide. They are woody and slightly longitudinally wrinkled when dry. The seeds are longitudinal and glabrous. The [[Glossary of botanical terms#funicle|funicle]] is expanded with 2–4 folds towards the seed,  and scarlet to orange.<ref name=plantnet/>

== Natural growing conditions ==
''Acacia salicina'' is found throughout [[Australia]], growing in regions receiving in excess of 1500mm annually in northern Queensland and as low as 100mm annually in central Australia. Its natural altitude range is from 50-300m above sea level.<ref name="species"/>  It does well in full sun exposure and tolerates frosts down to -6.7 deg. C (20 deg. F).<ref name="edu"/>

== Uses ==

* '''Erosion management''': ''Acacia salicina'' can be used to help stabilize riverbanks and other areas.<ref name="csu">[http://www.csu.edu.au/herbarium/acacsali_sws.html Acacia Salicina] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110515071728/http://www.csu.edu.au/herbarium/acacsali_sws.html |date=2011-05-15 }}, Csu.edu.au</ref>

* '''Fodder''': The tree's foliage and seed pods are important [[fodder]] for livestock during dry periods, since the tree can withstand drought quite well.<ref name="csu"/>  Its foliage and pods compare quite poorly to other fodders with regard to digestibility by [[livestock]].  This affects its available nutritional value.<ref name="www">{{Cite web|url=http://www.worldwidewattle.com/infogallery/utilisation/acaciasearch/pdf/salicina.pdf|title=Acacia Search|website=Worldwidewattle.com|access-date=15 March 2022}}</ref> The 1889 book ''The Useful Native Plants of Australia'' records that "The leaves are eaten by stock. This is another tree which is rapidly becoming scarce, owing to the partiality of stock to it."<ref name="J. H. Maiden 1889">{{cite book | author=J. H. Maiden | year=1889 | title=The useful native plants of Australia : Including Tasmania | publisher= Turner and Henderson, Sydney | url=https://primo-slnsw.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=SLNSW_ALMA21105097830002626&context=L&vid=SLNSW&search_scope=EEA&tab=default_tab&lang=en_US}}</ref>

* '''Food''': The seeds are edible.<ref name="csu"/>

* '''Landscaping''': ''A. salicina'' is excellent for [[landscaping]] in dry areas.<ref name="csu"/>

* '''Tannin''': The bark has a high [[tannin]] content.<ref name="csu"/>

* '''Wood''': The wood is very hard and it is used in making fine [[furniture]].<ref name="csu"/> At one time, the tree's wood was used in the manufacture of [[axle]]s for wagon wheels. ''A. salicina's'' wood burns well and makes good fuel.<ref name="csu"/> Its calorific content is 18900kJ/kg dry mass.<ref name="www"/> The tree produces seed and timber for woodworking in as little as five years after planting.<ref>[http://www.dpi.vic.gov.au/CA256F310024B628/0/E37E9A13CF973970CA256F9A008064F9/$File/Issue+27+Autumn+2003.pdf Victorian Landcare & Catchment Management], Autumn 2003 Issue 27 p. 8</ref>

* '''Other uses''': The bark has been traditionally put to use by [[Indigenous Australians]] as a [[toxin]] for [[fishing]].<ref name="csu"/>  The leaves of ''A. salicina'' are thought to be psychoactive, since indigenous Australians "burn its leaves and smoke the ash to obtain a state of inebriation."<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QN78GmmPGBQC&dq=acacia+alkaloids&pg=PA183|title=Handbook of Medicinal Plants|page=183|first1=Zohara|last1=Yaniv|first2=Uriel|last2=Bachrach|date=25 July 2005|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9781560229957 |access-date=15 March 2022|via=Google Books}}</ref>

==Weed status==
''Acacia salicina'' spreads widely through seed dispersal, and individual trees can rapidly form thickets through production of adventitious shoots from the root system. The species has become a significant weed over some of its native<ref name="www"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nativevegetation.nsw.gov.au/p/fact_sheet_9_list.pdf |title=Listed invasive native species by Catchment Management Authority |access-date=2014-01-06 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080719234214/http://www.nativevegetation.nsw.gov.au/p/fact_sheet_9_list.pdf |archive-date=2008-07-19 }}</ref> and introduced range.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://invasive.m-fuukei.jp/sdetail.php?g=Acacia&s=salicina|title=Invasive Plants Database|website=Invasive.m-fuukei.jp|access-date=15 March 2022}}</ref>
